subtitle: Prefixes that never split, and the same spelling for two verbs
words.intro: A German driving licence costs several thousand euros, takes months and is a rite of passage. It also contains a famous grammatical trap: *umfahren* can mean to drive round a thing, or to run it over.

grammar[0].fact: Prefixes change what a verb means, so English has to use a different word: *kommen, bekommen, verkommen, entkommen, umkommen*. One root, five lives. *Bekommen* doesn’t mean become, as you’ll have discovered, sooner or later, in a restaurant.

grammar[1].fact: The two verbs differ only in stress, and in speech that’s all you get. *Er setzt mich über* means he ferries me across. *Er übersetzt mich* means he translates me. Germans find this fine, and they tell the old driving-school joke at every opportunity.

document.intro: A real sample of a German licence, with its numbered fields. Its owner is the most famous person in Germany who doesn’t exist.
document.fact: Erika Mustermann appears on German sample documents and forms. Her surname means, roughly, *Pattern-man*. The field numbers are the same across the EU.

reading.intro: Maya is taking her driving test in Germany, for the third time. The examiner, Herr Kolb, sits in the back and doesn’t speak. Her instructor, Herr Sommer, is beside her. It’s going well. There’s a line of cones ahead, and a post at the end of it.
reading.photos[1].caption: Der Leitkegel: umfahren. Betonung auf „fah“.
reading.fact: A German licence typically costs thousands of euros, with lessons, night drives, motorway drives, a first-aid course and an eye test. A good share of candidates fail the theory test the first time.
